week_headline: Liver health and diet-cancer links dominate nutrition headlines as researchers spotlight specific foods and amino acids

top10.claim: Oxford audience invited to hear scientist research on diet
top10.verdict: Oxford researchers do present diet and nutrition science to public audiences, and science communication events are genuinely valuable. Without knowing which specific research is being shared, we can't score the underlying science — but Oxford's nutrition work is generally rigorous and peer-reviewed. The headline itself is informational rather than a health claim, so the real question is what was actually presented.
top10.verdict_highlight: The science matters more than the venue
sources: University of Oxford Nuffield Department of Population Health
top10.global_opinion: In the UK, public science lectures are a respected tradition and Oxford carries significant credibility. In the US, public trust in academic institutions varies more by political leaning. In many parts of Europe, university-led public health messaging is treated as a primary source of dietary guidance.
top10.brit_take: An Oxford lecture on diet sounds lovely — though one suspects the biscuits at the interval are doing more harm than good.

top10.claim: Study : Arginine deficiency may weaken immune system – NaturalNews . com
top10.verdict: Arginine is a real amino acid that genuinely plays a role in immune function, particularly in T-cell activity and wound healing — that part is science. But NaturalNews.com is a notoriously unreliable source that routinely exaggerates findings to sell supplements. True arginine deficiency is rare in people eating a normal diet, and most healthy adults get plenty from meat, nuts, and legumes. Don't let the kernel of truth pull you toward the supplement aisle.
top10.verdict_highlight: Real amino acid, unreliable source pushing supplements
sources: NIH – National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
Journal of Nutrition – arginine and immune function
Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
top10.global_opinion: In the US, arginine supplements are freely marketed and NaturalNews-style sites have a significant following. The EU's EFSA has approved only limited health claims for arginine, reflecting a more cautious regulatory stance. In Japan and South Korea, amino acid supplementation is mainstream but typically guided by clinical evidence rather than wellness blogs.
top10.brit_take: NaturalNews recommending supplements is a bit like a chip shop recommending salad — technically possible, but you know what they're really selling.

top10.claim: Scientists Say This 1 Food May Combat Fatty Liver Disease
top10.verdict: There is genuine emerging research linking certain foods — particularly coffee, oily fish rich in omega-3s, and foods high in vitamin E — to reduced liver fat and inflammation in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). However, no single food is a treatment, and the phrase 'this 1 food' is classic clickbait framing that oversimplifies real but modest findings. Lifestyle changes including overall diet quality, exercise, and weight management remain the best-supported approach.
top10.verdict_highlight: No single food fixes fatty liver disease
sources: Journal of Hepatology – NAFLD dietary interventions
NEJM – non-alcoholic fatty liver disease review
top10.global_opinion: In the Mediterranean region, olive oil and fish-heavy diets are already associated with lower NAFLD rates and are actively studied for liver protection. In the US, where NAFLD affects roughly 25% of adults, there is strong research interest but also heavy supplement marketing around the condition. The WHO recognises NAFLD as a growing global burden, with dietary intervention as a core management strategy.
top10.brit_take: If 'this 1 food' turns out to be coffee, the British public will be quietly relieved they've been medicating themselves for decades.

top10.claim: Fatty food raises risk of colorectal cancer
top10.verdict: There is solid evidence that diets high in processed and red meats — both of which tend to be high in saturated fat — are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk, and the WHO's IARC classifies processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen. However, 'fatty food' is a broad term that lumps together very different things: the fat in salmon or avocado behaves very differently in the body than the fat in a processed sausage. The risk is real but the framing is imprecise.
top10.verdict_highlight: Processed meat risk is real; 'fatty food' is too broad
sources: WHO – IARC Monographs on processed meat
Lancet Oncology – red meat and colorectal cancer
Cancer Research UK – bowel cancer risk factors
top10.global_opinion: In the UK, Cancer Research UK and the NHS both clearly advise limiting processed and red meat for bowel cancer prevention. In the US, the American Cancer Society echoes this but faces pushback from meat industry lobbying. In countries like Argentina and Uruguay with very high red meat consumption, colorectal cancer rates are notably elevated, lending weight to the association.
top10.brit_take: Telling the British public that fatty food raises cancer risk is brave — especially when the Sunday roast is considered a cultural institution.
